source_text: Εἶτ᾿ ἀπαντᾷ ἑαυτῷ, ὡς βούλεται· οὕτω δ᾿ οὐ μόνος ἱστόρηται ἐπιδεδημηκέναι τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων. ὡς καὶ τοὺς προφάσει τῆς διδασκαλίας τοῦ ὀνόματος Ἰησοῦ ἀποστάντας τοῦ δημιουργοῦ ὡς ἐλάττονος καὶ προσεληλυθότας ὡς κρείττονί τινι θεῷ καὶ πατρὶ τοῦ ἐπιδημήσαντος φάσκειν ὅτι καὶ πρὸ τούτου ἐπεδήμησάν τινες ἀπὸ τοῦ δημιουργοῦ τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἐπεὶ δὲ φιλαλήθως τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον ἐξετάζομεν, φήσομεν ὅτι ὁ Μαρκίωνος γνώριμος Ἀπελλῆς, αἱρέσεώς τινος γενόμενος πατὴρ καὶ μῦθον ἡγούμενος εἶναι τὰ Ἰουδαίων γράμματα. φησὶν ὅτι μόνος οὗτος ἐπιδεδήμηκε τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων. οὐδὲ πρὸς ἐκεῖνον οὖν, λέγοντα μόνον ἐπιδεδημηκέναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, εὐλόγως ἂν ὁ Κέλσος φέροι τὰ περὶ τοῦ καὶ ἄλλους ἐληλυθέναι, ἀπιστοῦντα. ὡς προείπομεν, ταῖς παραδοξότερα ἀπαγγελλούσαις Ἰουδαίων γραφαῖς· πολλῷ δὲ πλέον οὐ προσήσεται ἅπερ ἔοικε παρακούσας ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν τῷ Ἐνὼχ γεγραμμένων τεθεικέναι ὁ Κέλσος. οὐδεὶς τοίνυν ἐλέγχει ἡμᾶς ψευδομένους καὶ τὰ ἐναντία τιθέντας, ὅτι τε μόνος ἦλθεν ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν καὶ ὅτι, ἐπεὶ ἄλλοι πολλοὶ πολλάκις ἐληλύθασι. πάνυ δὲ συγκεχυμένως ἐν τῇ περὶ τῶν ἐληλυθότων πρὸς ἀνθρώπους ἀγγέλων ἐξετάσει τίθησι τὰ ἀτρανώτως ἐλθόντα εἰς αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν τῷ Ἐνὼχ γεγραμμένων· ἅτινα οὐδ᾿ αὐτὰ φαίνεται ἀναγνοὺς οὐδὲ γνωρίσας ὅτι ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις οὐ πάνυ φέρεται ὡς θεῖα τὰ ἐπιγεγραμμένα τοῦ Ἐνὼχ βιβλία· ὅθεν νομισθείη ἂν ἐῤῥιφέναι τὸ ὁμοῦ ἑξήκοντα ἢ ἑβδομήκοντα καταβεβηκέναι, κακοὺς γενομένους.
pass_a_gloss: Then he replies (ἀπαντάω) to himself, as he wishes (βούλομαι); but thus he is not recorded (ἱστορέω) alone to have visited (ἐπιδημέω) the race of men; so that even those who on pretext (πρόφασις) of the teaching of the name of Jesus stood away (ἀφίστημι) from the Creator (δημιουργός) as lesser (ἐλάσσων) and went over (προσέρχομαι) as to some greater (κρείττων) God and Father of the one who visited, say that even before this one some visited the race of men from the Creator. But since with love of truth we examine the things in the passage (τόπος), we will say that Apelles, the disciple (γνώριμος) of Marcion, become father of a certain heresy (αἵρεσις) and considering (ἡγέομαι) the writings (γράμματα) of the Jews to be myth (μῦθος), says that this one alone has visited the race of men. Not even against him, then, saying that Jesus alone visited from God to men, would Celsus reasonably (εὐλόγως) bring the things about others too having come, he disbelieving (ἀπιστέω), as we said before, the Scriptures (γραφαί) of the Jews which report more marvellous things (παραδοξότερα); and much more he will not accept (προσίεμαι) what Celsus seems, having misheard (παρακούω) from the things written in Enoch, to have set down (τίθημι). No one then convicts (ἐλέγχω) us lying and setting down contraries (ἐναντία), both that our Saviour alone came and that, since many others often have come. But very confusedly (συγκεχυμένως) in the examination about the angels who have come to men he sets down the things that came to him indistinctly (ἀτρανώτως) from the things written in Enoch; which he appears neither to have read (ἀναγιγνώσκω) nor to have known that in the churches the books inscribed (ἐπιγράφω) of Enoch are not at all carried (οὐ πάνυ φέρεται) as divine (θεῖα); whence he might be thought to have flung out (ῥίπτω) the 'sixty or seventy came down together, having become wicked'.

pass_b_english: Then he answers himself as he pleases. But in fact Christ is not recorded as the only one to have visited the human race. So true is this that even those who, using the teaching of the name of Jesus as a pretext, have turned away from the Creator as lesser and gone over to some God as greater and as Father of the one who came, say that even before him some visited the human race from the Creator.

But since we are examining this passage with a love of truth, we will say that Apelles, the disciple of Marcion, who became the father of a certain heresy and regarded the writings of the Jews as myth, says that this one alone has visited the human race. So not even against him, though he says that Jesus alone has come from God to men, could Celsus reasonably bring the argument that others too have come; for, as we said before, Apelles does not believe the Jewish Scriptures, which report rather marvellous things. Much less will he accept what Celsus seems to have set down after mishearing what is written in Enoch.

No one, then, convicts us of lying and of asserting contradictory things, as though we said both that our Saviour alone came and that many others have often come. But in his inquiry into the angels who have come to men, Celsus sets down in great confusion what reached him indistinctly from what is written in Enoch. He does not appear even to have read these writings, nor to have known that in the churches the books inscribed with Enoch's name are not generally received as divine. That is why he might be thought to have tossed out the claim that sixty or seventy came down together, having become wicked.
notes: οὕτω δ᾿ οὐ μόνος ἱστόρηται ἐπιδεδημηκέναι: the subject is unexpressed; 'Christ' (from the end of 5.53) is supplied. ὡς καὶ τοὺς ... φάσκειν is consecutive ('so that even those ... say'), rendered 'So true is this that even those ...'. The group described (who left the Creator for a higher God and Father of Jesus) are Marcionite-type teachers; Origen names Apelles, Marcion's disciple, as the exception who says Jesus alone came. ὅτι τε μόνος ἦλθεν ... καὶ ὅτι, ἐπεὶ ἄλλοι πολλοὶ πολλάκις ἐληλύθασι is corrupt in the staged text (ἐπεί has no clause to govern); rendered by sense 'both that ... and that many others have often come'. οὐ πάνυ φέρεται ὡς θεῖα may mean 'by no means received' or more softly 'not generally received'; the review gives the softer sense, since Origen himself cites Enoch elsewhere with reserve ('if anyone accepts the book') and so does not treat it as wholly rejected. The staged text has full stops after γράμματα and ἀπιστοῦντα that break single sentences; read as running on. Enoch is not Scripture for this edition, so no inline citation is given; the 'sixty or seventy' is Celsus's figure, not in extant 1 Enoch. Review: the closing τὸ ... καταβεβηκέναι, κακοὺς γενομένους is Origen's restatement (Celsus wrote ἐλθεῖν in 5.52), so it is no longer printed in quotation marks; ἐῤῥιφέναι 'tossed out' (the old 'at random' was an addition). 'by saying both' made the clause read as if the accuser said both; now 'as though we said both'. ἐλάττονος 'lesser' (not 'an inferior being'); ὡς governs both 'greater' and 'Father'.
